items.question:
An operations excellence lead at a precision-parts manufacturer uploads a 45-page process audit PDF and asks Claude to identify gaps. The response correctly flags three non-conformances from the document but also states: "Industry best practice recommends a maximum cycle-time variance of ±8% for Class II machined components." This figure appears nowhere in the uploaded audit.

How should the lead classify this second claim?

options.A: A grounded inference derived from context clues within the uploaded PDF.
options.B: A formatting artefact that drifted in from a different section of the audit document.
options.C: A parametric claim drawn from the model's training data rather than from the supplied document.
options.D: A calibrated estimate interpolated from the three non-conformances found in the audit.

items.question:
An actuarial associate at a specialty insurer uses Claude to draft commentary for a quarterly reserve report. The output includes: "Historical data shows third-party liability claims in this segment close within 18 months at a rate of 73%." The associate's own reserving system shows the actual 18-month closure rate for this book is 58%.

What property of Claude's output does this scenario MOST clearly illustrate?

options.A: Claude applied the wrong statistical formula when computing the closure rate from the uploaded claims data.
options.B: Claude's response reflects a system-instruction conflict that substituted a generic industry figure for the actual data.
options.C: Claude's training cutoff means its figure reflects an older industry benchmark that no longer matches current experience.
options.D: Claude generated a plausible-sounding statistic from training memory that does not correspond to any actual dataset.

items.question:
A regulatory affairs associate at a mid-size pharma company uses Claude to prepare a four-page summary of competitor product approvals for an internal strategy meeting. The summary covers approved indications, clinical trial outcomes, manufacturing site information, and general disease-area background for six products.

Which TWO content categories carry the HIGHEST fabrication risk and should be prioritised for source-checking? (Choose TWO)

options.A: Specific approval dates and regulatory submission numbers attributed to each competitor product.
options.B: General background descriptions of the disease areas addressed by the six products.
options.C: Named clinical trial identifiers and precise efficacy percentages attributed to published study results.
options.D: The section headings and document structure used to organise the summary.
options.E: Brief explanations of how each regulatory agency operates in general terms.

items.question:
A category manager at a national grocery retailer pastes a 12-page supplier contract into a Claude conversation and asks for a payment-terms summary. The response accurately extracts the net-60 payment schedule, early-payment discount percentage, and dispute-resolution clause — all of which appear verbatim in the contract. The manager files the summary without further checking.

Which statement BEST characterises the reliability of this output?

options.A: The output is grounded in the supplied document, so each extracted claim is traceable and verifiable against the source text.
options.B: The output is reliable because Claude applies formal legal reasoning to contracts and rarely makes extraction errors on structured documents.
options.C: The output requires external legal review before use because summaries of contracts are inherently unreliable regardless of extraction accuracy.
options.D: The output is unreliable because Claude cannot access external databases to validate these terms against market benchmarks.

items.question:
A communications director at a government transport agency uses Claude to draft a press release about a new rail safety initiative. The draft includes a direct quote from the agency's CEO: "We are entering a new era of rail safety that will save hundreds of lives annually." The director knows the CEO has not been briefed on the initiative and has made no such statement.

What is the PRIMARY risk created by this output?

options.A: The quote is longer than agency style guidelines allow for attributed statements in official releases.
options.B: Claude fabricated a direct quote attributed to a real named individual, creating reputational and legal exposure if published.
options.C: The quote understates the initiative's impact and should be replaced with more measurable language.
options.D: The quote is accurate in substance but the CEO should be listed as secondary attribution rather than primary.

items.question:
A research administrator at a large university asks Claude to populate a grant application bibliography. Claude produces 18 formatted citations. Checking each one, the administrator finds: 14 are real papers with correct metadata; 3 are real papers but list incorrect author names; and 1 does not correspond to any paper that can be located in any database.

Which hallucination type does the ONE non-existent citation BEST represent?

options.A: Staleness — Claude's training data contains a retracted version of the paper that was removed from databases.
options.B: Omission — Claude failed to include a relevant real paper and substituted a placeholder citation.
options.C: Misattribution — Claude assigned a real paper's content and title to the wrong author team.
options.D: Fabrication — Claude generated a citation with no corresponding real source.

items.question:
A strategy consultant preparing a due-diligence memo asks Claude to name the top five consulting firms that advised on telecoms M&A transactions over the past three years, with brief deal examples. The response names five firms with specific transactions. The consultant's firm's deal database shows two of the five named firms had no involvement in telecom advisory during that period.

Which characteristic of this prompt MOST directly caused the fabricated firm names?

options.A: The prompt requested a ranked top-five list, forcing Claude to fill positions even with insufficient information.
options.B: The prompt was too short; a more detailed prompt with explicit instructions would have prevented the error.
options.C: The prompt asked Claude to think through the answer step by step, which can introduce extra generative steps.
options.D: The prompt requested specific facts about real named entities without supplying grounding material, so Claude drew on parametric memory.

items.question:
A managing editor at a digital news outlet reviews a Claude-assisted draft about a city's new urban planning initiative. The article includes: a general explanation of what zoning regulations are; a direct quote attributed to the city planning commissioner; the exact council-approved project budget; and a brief description of why urban planners value mixed-use zoning.

Which TWO content types carry the HIGHEST fabrication risk and should be verified first? (Choose TWO)

options.A: The general explanation of what zoning regulations are and how they work.
options.B: The direct quote attributed to the city planning commissioner.
options.C: The brief description of why urban planners value mixed-use zoning.
options.D: The exact dollar amount of the council-approved project budget.
options.E: The article's headline summarising the initiative in a single sentence.

items.question:
A trade compliance coordinator at a global freight forwarder asks Claude when a set of tariff changes for steel imports took effect. Claude states the changes became effective on a specific date and references the regulation by number. When the coordinator checks the official government trade portal, the actual effective date is three months earlier than what Claude stated.

Which action should the coordinator take FIRST?

options.A: Use the official government portal date for all compliance purposes and flag Claude's response as unverified for regulatory date queries.
options.B: Accept Claude's date because the regulation number was correct, suggesting the date is a minor transcription error rather than a fabrication.
options.C: Ask Claude to regenerate the answer with a higher reasoning effort to obtain the correct date.
options.D: Escalate to IT to determine whether Claude's training data was corrupted before relying on any further outputs.

items.question:
A regulatory affairs analyst at an oil and gas company is reviewing a Claude-generated compliance briefing. The briefing contains four types of claims: (1) a description of how emissions monitoring generally works; (2) the specific consent decree number for a competitor's 2022 EPA settlement; (3) the current price of carbon offset credits; and (4) a general list of pollutants subject to reporting requirements under Clean Air Act Title V.

Which claim type carries the HIGHEST hallucination risk and should be verified first?

options.A: The description of how emissions monitoring generally works.
options.B: The specific consent decree number for the competitor's EPA settlement.
options.C: The current price of carbon offset credits.
options.D: The general list of pollutants subject to Title V reporting requirements.

items.question:
A development director at a small non-profit preparing a grant application asks Claude to supply impact statistics for the literacy sector. Claude's response includes: "Research consistently shows that early-childhood reading interventions improve third-grade proficiency scores by an average of 34% when delivered by trained community educators." The director cannot find this statistic in any peer-reviewed source.

What is the MOST appropriate immediate action?

options.A: Use the statistic in the application but add a footnote stating it is an internal estimate derived from program data.
options.B: Ask Claude to regenerate with a different prompt to see if it produces a source for the same statistic.
options.C: Discard the statistic and locate a real published figure from a peer-reviewed source or reputable sector body.
options.D: Round the figure to 35% and use it, as minor rounding is acceptable in grant narrative context.

items.question:
A solution architect at a telecoms company is evaluating two approaches for a Claude-based product-information chatbot: (A) uploading the product catalogue as a PDF to a Project knowledge base, versus (B) relying on Claude's general training knowledge about the company's products. The catalogue is updated quarterly.

Which statement BEST explains why approach A is more reliable for factual product claims?

options.A: Approach A uses a more powerful model variant that is specifically optimised for document retrieval tasks.
options.B: Approach A uses a longer context window that inherently reduces hallucination probability on all types of claims.
options.C: Approach A and B are equivalent for stable product facts; approach A only adds value for pricing and availability data.
options.D: Approach A grounds responses in the actual catalogue content, making claims verifiable and current, whereas approach B relies on parametric memory that may be outdated or incomplete for proprietary product details.

items.question:
A VP of Brand Marketing at an international hotel group asks Claude to produce a 10-slide competitive benchmarking deck. The deck includes: guest-satisfaction survey scores attributed to specific competitor brands; a direct quote from a competitor CEO's investor call; a statistic from a named industry body's annual report; general descriptions of each brand's positioning strategy; and Claude's own assessment of market trends.

Which THREE content types carry the HIGHEST hallucination risk and require source verification before the deck is shared? (Choose THREE)

options.A: Guest-satisfaction survey scores attributed to specific competitor brands.
options.B: General descriptions of each competitor brand's positioning strategy.
options.C: The direct quote attributed to a competitor CEO from a named investor call.
options.D: Claude's own qualitative assessment of current market trends.
options.E: The statistic attributed to the named industry body's annual report.

items.question:
A fund operations analyst at an asset manager asks Claude about the reporting requirements under a specific derivatives regulation that was significantly amended 14 months ago. Claude's response accurately describes the pre-amendment requirements but does not mention the amendment at all. The requirements described are consistent with the regulation as it existed two years ago.

Which failure mode BEST describes this output?

options.A: Knowledge-cutoff staleness — Claude's training data does not include the amendment, so it accurately reflects an older version of the requirements.
options.B: Fabrication — Claude generated a plausible-sounding regulatory description that does not match any real version of the regulation.
options.C: Misattribution — Claude applied the requirements from a different regulation to the one that was asked about.
options.D: Omission error — Claude selectively ignored the amendment to produce a shorter, simpler response.

items.question:
A pharmacy benefits coordinator at a 400-person self-insured employer reviews a Claude-generated formulary analysis. The analysis mentions that Drug X "has a documented interaction with Drug Y that can cause QT prolongation in patients with pre-existing cardiac conditions." The coordinator checks three clinical drug-interaction databases and finds no such interaction documented for this drug pair.

What is the MOST appropriate response to this finding?

options.A: Accept the interaction warning provisionally and flag it for review at the next quarterly formulary committee meeting.
options.B: Accept the output because three databases may all share the same data gap, and a model trained on broader literature might be correct.
options.C: Ask the plan's pharmacy benefit manager to run the same query in their system to check whether their tools confirm the interaction.
options.D: Remove the interaction claim from the analysis and verify all other clinical assertions in the document against authoritative pharmacological sources.

items.question:
A quality systems engineer at an automotive components manufacturer asks Claude to summarise the calibration requirements for torque measurement equipment under a relevant quality standard. The response includes several requirements the engineer recognises as accurate, but also cites a specific clause number ("Clause 7.1.5.2, Sub-section (d)") that the engineer cannot locate in their copy of the standard. The engineer has already confirmed that the clause number does not appear in the standard's table of contents.

What should the engineer do NEXT?

options.A: File a corrective action report against the Claude deployment and suspend its use pending investigation.
options.B: Accept the other recognised requirements as correct and flag only the unlocatable clause for a later review cycle.
options.C: Verify each requirement in the response against the actual standard text before relying on any of the output for compliance documentation.
options.D: Ask Claude to regenerate the summary with a request to include page numbers so the clause can be located.

items.question:
An insurance claims adjuster uses Claude to draft a summary of a first-party property claim. The summary includes four types of content: a general description of how actual-cash-value calculations work; the policyholder's name and claim number (copied from the adjuster's notes); a statement that "replacement cost for residential HVAC systems of this type typically ranges from $4,200 to $6,800"; and the date the claim was reported.

Which content type carries the HIGHEST risk of containing a fabricated or unverifiable figure?

options.A: The general description of how actual-cash-value calculations work.
options.B: The policyholder's name and claim number copied from the adjuster's notes.
options.C: The date the claim was reported.
options.D: The replacement cost range for residential HVAC systems of this type.

items.question:
A clinical data manager at a large pharma company reviews a Claude-generated summary of a Phase III trial protocol for a competitor's asset. The summary appears well-structured and detailed. The data manager wants to determine which elements are most likely to contain fabricated information.

Which TWO indicators in a clinical summary MOST reliably signal that content may have been fabricated rather than sourced? (Choose TWO)

options.A: The summary uses medical terminology consistently throughout the document.
options.B: A specific NCT registration number is cited that does not appear on ClinicalTrials.gov.
options.C: A precise primary endpoint result (e.g., 47.3% response rate, p=0.003) is attributed to a named trial that cannot be located in published literature.
options.D: The summary describes the trial design using CONSORT-compliant structure and terminology.
options.E: The summary mentions the geographic regions where trial sites were located.

items.question:
A business analyst at a mid-size retailer uploads Q3 sales data as a spreadsheet and asks Claude to identify the three top-performing product categories. Claude correctly identifies the categories from the data and states their revenue figures. The response also includes: "Category managers typically allocate 15–20% of their discretionary budget to top-performing categories in Q4 to capitalise on momentum." This second claim is not in the uploaded spreadsheet.

How should the analyst treat the budget allocation claim?

options.A: As an irrelevant detail that Claude added for context and can be safely ignored without verification.
options.B: As a grounded inference because Claude derived it from the revenue patterns shown in the uploaded spreadsheet.
options.C: As a reliable benchmark because Claude's training on retail industry sources makes its percentage ranges accurate.
options.D: As a parametric claim from training data that requires independent verification before use in planning documents.

items.question:
A policy analyst at a federal agency asks Claude to summarise the provisions of a specific environmental regulation. Claude's response correctly describes the regulation's general purpose and key obligations, but cites it as "Section 12(c)(4) of the Clean Water Act Amendments of 2019." The analyst's legal reference tools show no 2019 amendments to the Clean Water Act exist.

What does this error MOST likely indicate?

options.A: The analyst's legal reference tools are outdated and have not indexed the 2019 amendment package yet.
options.B: Claude fabricated a specific citation form — a year and section number — that does not correspond to any real legislative event.
options.C: Claude's training cutoff occurred before 2019, preventing it from accurately describing post-cutoff legislation.
options.D: The provision exists under a different statute that Claude incorrectly identified as the Clean Water Act.

items.question:
A curriculum developer at a large university extension program asks Claude to draft learning objectives for a module on behavioural economics, including references to key research findings. The draft cites several well-known studies accurately but also references: "a 2021 study by Chen and Nakamura published in the Journal of Behavioural Decision Making, which found that loss aversion diminishes significantly after age 65." The developer cannot find this study in the journal's archives or any academic database.

Beyond removing this specific citation, what is the MOST important action for the developer?

options.A: Switch to a research-focused tool that has live database access before continuing module development.
options.B: Ask Claude to provide the DOI number for the study so it can be more easily located in the database.
options.C: Limit future academic citation requests to pre-2000 research, where Claude's training data is more reliable.
options.D: Review all other research citations in the draft against academic databases, since one fabricated citation indicates the output may mix real and fabricated sources.

items.question:
An internal auditor at a professional services firm uses Claude to draft a process-risk matrix for a client's accounts-payable function. The matrix was produced without any client documents uploaded. It lists 12 control activities and assigns a risk rating to each. The auditor finds the matrix looks familiar and professional.

Which content in the matrix carries the GREATEST verification burden before it is shared with the client?

options.A: The general descriptions of risk categories such as payment fraud, duplicate invoices, and segregation-of-duties gaps.
options.B: The formatting of the matrix and the column headers used to organise the information.
options.C: The professional tone and language register of the document.
options.D: The specific risk ratings assigned to each control activity and any implied thresholds or benchmarks used in those ratings.

items.question:
A corporate communications analyst at a publicly traded consumer goods company drafts an investor relations update with Claude's assistance. The draft contains two items the analyst cannot verify: a direct quote attributed to a competitor's CFO from their last earnings call, and a specific revenue growth percentage attributed to a named analyst firm's sector report.

Which TWO risks are MOST directly created by including these unverified items in the investor relations update? (Choose TWO)

options.A: Publishing a fabricated quote attributed to a real named executive could constitute misrepresentation and create legal exposure.
options.B: The document will not pass internal spell-check tools if it contains fabricated content.
options.C: Investor relations teams are required by style guides to avoid direct competitor quotes entirely.
options.D: Citing a non-existent analyst report in a public investor communication could mislead investors and attract regulatory scrutiny.
options.E: Fabricated content in investor relations updates automatically triggers an earnings restatement process.

items.question:
A procurement analyst at a third-party logistics provider asks Claude to draft a technical specification section for an RFP for warehouse management system software. Without any system requirements document uploaded, Claude generates detailed minimum RAM requirements, integration protocol specifications, and API throughput benchmarks. The technical team later notes that two of the API benchmarks Claude specified are implausibly high for the use case described.

Which statement BEST characterises what Claude produced?

options.A: Claude generated parametric technical specifications from training-data patterns that may not reflect the organisation's actual requirements or realistic benchmarks for this use case.
options.B: Claude applied a formal requirements-analysis method and produced specifications that are industry-standard even if not specifically tailored.
options.C: The implausible benchmarks indicate Claude's training data was limited to large-enterprise systems that do not apply to this scale of deployment.
options.D: Claude intentionally generated aspirational benchmarks to give the organisation negotiating leverage with potential vendors.

items.question:
A project controls lead at a renewable energy developer reviews a Claude-generated project risk register. The register contains 15 risk entries. Entry 9 states: "Turbine foundation settlement risk — probability: 12%, impact: $2.3M, risk score: 276." Entry 12 states: "Planning permission delay — likelihood: high, impact: schedule slip of 3–6 months." The lead is concerned about relying on Claude's output for the project's risk management plan.

Which entry warrants GREATER verification scrutiny and why?

options.A: Entry 12, because schedule delays are more consequential than cost risks for this project type.
options.B: Entry 9, because specific numeric probability and cost figures are parametric claims that were not derived from any supplied project data.
options.C: Both entries equally, because all content in a risk register generated without project data should be treated as illustrative only.
options.D: Entry 12, because qualitative ratings like 'high likelihood' are harder to verify than quantitative figures.

items.question:
A program evaluator at a non-profit focused on workforce development asks Claude to summarise evidence for the effectiveness of mentorship programs. Claude cites five studies supporting the effectiveness of formal mentorship. When the evaluator checks one citation — "Johnson, T. & Williams, R. (2020). Structured mentorship and six-month employment outcomes. Journal of Applied Workforce Studies, 14(3), 78–95" — it cannot be located in any database.

What is the MOST appropriate response?

options.A: Use the summary but note in the document that one citation could not be verified, pending a follow-up search.
options.B: Accept the unlocatable citation as probably real but behind a library paywall; proceed with the summary.
options.C: Discard all five citations and conduct an independent literature search to find real, verifiable sources for the claims.
options.D: Ask Claude to provide the ISSN number for the journal to assist in locating it through a library system.

items.question:
A product manager at a telecoms operator uses Claude to analyse a 30-page customer satisfaction report that was uploaded as a PDF. The response includes: (1) the actual NPS score from the report (42); (2) a segment breakdown also from the report; and (3) the statement "B2B customers in regulated industries typically value reliability over price at a ratio of approximately 3:1." This third claim does not appear in the uploaded report.

A colleague asks whether the 3:1 ratio is reliable. What is the BEST answer?

options.A: Yes — the ratio came from the customer satisfaction report that was uploaded, so it is grounded and verifiable.
options.B: Possibly — it is a widely cited figure in B2B telecoms research and Claude's training likely draws on accurate industry literature.
options.C: Not necessarily — it is a parametric claim from training data that was not sourced from the uploaded report and requires independent verification.
options.D: No — Claude cannot produce reliable statements about customer preferences because it has no access to real-time survey data.

items.question:
A revenue director at a full-service hotel chain asks Claude to compile a competitive rate analysis for a new property launch. Without providing any market data or OTA screenshots, the director receives a response listing specific average daily rates for five competitor hotels, including seasonal ranges and occupancy-rate estimates.

Which THREE statements about this output are accurate? (Choose THREE)

options.A: The specific rate figures are grounded because Claude synthesised them from publicly available hotel booking sites during the query.
options.B: The specific ADR and occupancy figures are parametric claims that should not be used as the basis for pricing decisions without independent market data.
options.C: The output may reflect rate structures from Claude's training data that are outdated by months or years and do not represent current market conditions.
options.D: Because the figures were generated without grounding material, they have the same reliability as data from a professional rate-shopping tool.
options.E: Using these unverified figures in a pricing model creates risk of launching with rates that do not reflect actual competitive positioning.

items.question:
A compliance officer at a wealth management firm uses Claude to check whether a specific investment product still qualifies for preferential tax treatment under applicable rules. Claude's response confidently states it does, citing the relevant rules and thresholds. However, the firm's tax counsel notes that those rules were amended 18 months ago and the product no longer qualifies.

What is the MOST accurate characterisation of Claude's error?

options.A: Claude's training data reflects the pre-amendment rules, so it accurately described the older regulatory framework rather than the current one.
options.B: Claude fabricated the tax treatment qualification because it lacked any information about this specific product type.
options.C: Claude made a reasoning error in applying the tax rules rather than a knowledge error about their content.
options.D: Claude's system instructions directed it to provide optimistic compliance assessments rather than conservative ones.

items.question:
An HR business partner at a hospital network uses Claude to draft a response to an employee grievance about a flexible scheduling policy. The draft cites "Section 4.7(b) of the Joint Commission's 2023 Staff Scheduling and Retention Guidelines" as support for the employer's position. When the HR business partner checks, no such section or document exists in Joint Commission publications.

Beyond correcting this specific citation, what practice change would MOST directly prevent recurrence?

options.A: Switch from Claude to a different AI assistant that specialises in HR policy documents.
options.B: Limit Claude's use in HR contexts to administrative tasks only, prohibiting it from generating any regulatory references.
options.C: Ask Claude to rate its confidence in each citation on a scale of 1–10 before including it in a final document.
options.D: Provide the actual relevant policy documents and guidelines to Claude as context before asking it to draft regulatory references.

items.question:
A strategic sourcing manager at a consumer electronics manufacturer asks Claude to summarise the key terms in a supplier contract that was uploaded as a 80-page PDF. The summary correctly extracts the delivery terms and payment schedule. It also states: "The supplier's standard lead time for PCB assemblies of this specification is 14 days." The manager finds this lead time in the contract, but also notices that the summary states the force majeure clause requires 10 business days' written notice — a figure the manager believes may be incorrect.

How should the manager approach this discrepancy?

options.A: Accept the force majeure notice period as correct because most supply contracts use 10 business days as a standard term.
options.B: Assume the force majeure clause is incorrectly extracted because the model cannot accurately process legal language in long documents.
options.C: Check the force majeure clause in the actual contract to confirm the exact notice period, as the summary may have altered the specific figure.
options.D: Discard the entire summary and re-upload a shorter excerpt of the contract to avoid extraction errors.

items.question:
A product development lead at a specialty insurer is reviewing two Claude-generated market analysis statements. Statement 1: "Personal lines cyber insurance is a growing segment, with several carriers expanding their product offerings." Statement 2: "The personal lines cyber market grew 38.7% in gross written premium in the 12 months ended Q2 last year, with the top five carriers capturing 71% of that growth."

Which statement carries the HIGHER hallucination risk and why?

options.A: Statement 1, because general market growth claims are harder to verify than specific figures with defined time periods.
options.B: Both statements carry equal risk because neither cites a named source.
options.C: Statement 1, because vague descriptions are more likely to be generated from training patterns than precise statistics.
options.D: Statement 2, because specific percentages and time-bound market share figures are the claim type most likely to be generated from training patterns rather than sourced.

items.question:
A market access manager at a specialty pharma company receives a Claude-generated payer landscape summary. The summary covers reimbursement trends across five therapeutic areas. Several statements include precise numbers and attributed sources.

Which TWO characteristics of statistics in the summary MOST reliably indicate that a figure may have been fabricated rather than sourced? (Choose TWO)

options.A: A statistic is stated with a decimal-level precision (e.g., 23.4%) but cannot be located in the attributed source when that source is searched.
options.B: A statistic uses terminology that is standard in payer landscape analysis (e.g., 'prior authorisation rate,' 'formulary tier placement').
options.C: A statistic describes a trend that aligns with the manager's general understanding of the market.
options.D: A statistic is attributed to a named report that has a plausible-sounding title but cannot be found in the publishing organisation's document library.
options.E: A statistic appears in a section of the summary that covers a therapeutic area where the manager has less prior knowledge.

items.question:
An e-commerce operations manager at an online fashion retailer asks Claude to summarise a 60-page returns policy review document that was uploaded. The summary looks plausible but includes a customer satisfaction score of "84% satisfaction with the current returns process" that the manager is certain does not appear anywhere in the 60-page document — the review did not include customer survey data.

The manager has already confirmed the figure is absent from the uploaded document. What should the manager do NEXT?

options.A: Verify all other specific metrics and figures in the summary against the uploaded document before using any part of the output.
options.B: Delete the summary and start a new conversation, re-uploading the document without the suspicious metric in the prompt.
options.C: Accept the summary except for the identified metric and proceed, since one isolated error does not indicate systemic problems.
options.D: Ask Claude to identify which sections of the document contained customer satisfaction data to confirm whether the figure came from the text.

items.question:
An internal auditor at a county government office uses Claude to draft a report section on procurement fraud risks. The draft states: "According to the Government Accountability Office's 2023 Federal Procurement Integrity Report, 22% of procurement violations in local government involved sole-source contract abuse." The auditor cannot find any GAO report by that name or that statistic in GAO's publications database.

What BEST describes this output?

options.A: A stale citation — the report was published before the auditor's access to the GAO database was established.
options.B: A fabricated attribution — Claude generated a plausible-sounding GAO report name and specific statistic that do not correspond to a real publication.
options.C: A misattribution — the statistic is real but was published by a different government accountability body, not the GAO.
options.D: A summary error — the report exists but the statistic refers to federal government, not local government as stated in the draft.

items.question:
A career services advisor at a business school asks Claude about current starting salary ranges for data-science roles in financial services. Claude provides specific salary band figures. When the advisor compares them to a current salary survey published two months ago by a professional association, several of Claude's figures are 8–15% lower than the current market data.

What is the MOST accurate explanation for this discrepancy?

options.A: The figures differ because Claude is calibrated to provide conservative estimates to avoid setting unrealistic expectations.
options.B: The figures differ because the professional association survey samples larger employers that pay above-market rates.
options.C: The figures reflect market conditions at the time of Claude's training data and may predate the salary increases that occurred between that point and now.
options.D: The figures differ because Claude sampled a different geographic concentration of roles when generating the ranges.

items.question:
An L&D manager at a global professional services firm is building an onboarding module using Claude to draft content about industry-specific compliance requirements. A subject-matter expert reviews the draft and flags three statements that reference specific regulatory thresholds that have changed in the last 18 months. None of the SME's changes involve made-up information — just outdated figures.

Which statement BEST characterises the hallucination type the SME identified?

options.A: Fabrication — Claude generated regulatory thresholds that do not correspond to any current or historical requirement.
options.B: Misattribution — Claude applied thresholds from one regulatory regime to a different jurisdiction.
options.C: Confabulation — Claude produced confident output by blending real knowledge with invented details.
options.D: Staleness — Claude accurately described thresholds as they existed in its training data but those thresholds have since changed.

items.question:
A content strategy director at a digital media company is reviewing a Claude-generated thought-leadership piece that cites academic research. Two citations stand out: one references a paper by 'Martinez et al. (2022)' that cannot be found in Google Scholar, and another cites a 'Journal of Digital Communication Studies' that appears to have no publication history.

Which TWO conclusions are MOST supported by these findings? (Choose TWO)

options.A: Both citations indicate that the paper and the journal were likely generated by Claude rather than retrieved from real publications.
options.B: The citations are probably real but are published under different titles than how Claude described them.
options.C: The thought-leadership piece should not be published until all citations are verified against real academic sources.
options.D: The director should ask Claude to provide the DOI for the Martinez paper to help locate it in a database.
options.E: A missing journal implies Claude's training data had no information about this publication, not that the journal is fabricated.

items.question:
A contract manager at a 3PL logistics provider uploads a 95-page master service agreement and asks Claude to extract key commercial terms. The extraction looks accurate for payment terms and service levels, but includes a termination-for-convenience provision that states: "Either party may terminate with 30 days written notice." When the contract manager searches the actual agreement, the actual notice period is 90 days, not 30.

Which of the following BEST explains how this error arose and what it indicates?

options.A: Claude substituted a common industry default (30 days) for the actual contractual term, producing a plausible-but-incorrect specific figure from parametric memory rather than from the document.
options.B: Claude's document-processing limit prevented it from reading page 78 where the termination clause appeared, causing it to generate a placeholder value.
options.C: The 30-day notice period is the correct figure; the contract manager's recollection of the 90-day term is likely mistaken.
options.D: Claude's reasoning applied the shortest reasonable notice period to avoid presenting unfavourable terms to the requesting party.

items.question:
A corporate sustainability officer at a utility company needs to prepare a summary of the company's Scope 1 and Scope 2 emissions for an investor ESG questionnaire. She considers two approaches: (A) pasting the relevant sections of the company's most recent sustainability report and internal emissions inventory directly into Claude's context and asking it to synthesise the answer, or (B) asking Claude to write the summary based on general knowledge of the utility sector's emissions profile.

Why is approach A significantly more reliable for this specific task?

options.A: Approach A uses a different model architecture that is specifically optimised for numerical data synthesis.
options.B: Approach A is more reliable only for Scope 2 data; Scope 1 data is stable enough that training-data knowledge is sufficient.
options.C: Approach A and B are equally reliable because Scope 1 and 2 emissions methodologies are standardised across the sector.
options.D: Approach A grounds Claude's response in the company's actual reported figures, making the output traceable and specific to this organisation rather than drawn from sector-level training patterns.

items.question:
A grant manager at a non-profit providing housing support services asks Claude to draft an impact section for a major donor report. Without any programme data or outcome records supplied, Claude writes: "Your investment enabled 847 individuals to secure stable housing, with 91% maintaining housing stability at 12 months." The non-profit's actual outcome data shows 312 individuals served with a 78% stability rate.

Why is this a significant risk?

options.A: The figures Claude generated are overstated and would misrepresent programme outcomes to a donor who funded based on those results.
options.B: The 91% stability figure is implausibly high and will be immediately recognised as fabricated by an experienced donor.
options.C: Grant reporting requires a specific format that Claude did not follow, making the figures unusable regardless of accuracy.
options.D: The figures are acceptable as approximations because donor reports are narrative documents, not audited financial statements.

items.question:
A strategy analyst at a mobile telecoms operator is preparing a board presentation on network performance benchmarks. Claude provides specific figures: "Industry leading operators achieve 99.97% network availability and a mean time to restore of under 4.2 hours for P1 incidents." The analyst wants to use these figures as targets, but the network operations team says they cannot find a published source for these specific benchmarks.

How should the analyst treat these figures before including them in the board presentation?

options.A: Use the figures as-is because they represent Claude's synthesis of widely available industry data and are therefore reliable.
options.B: Use the figures but label them as 'Claude-estimated benchmarks' to provide transparency about their origin.
options.C: Discard the figures and use the analyst's own judgement about appropriate performance targets instead.
options.D: Verify the figures against published industry benchmarks from GSMA, analyst firms, or operator earnings disclosures before presenting them to the board.

items.question:
A brand standards manager at a major hospitality franchise asks Claude to draft guidance reminding franchisees about required visual identity standards. Without uploading the official brand guidelines, Claude produces a detailed memo referencing specific pantone codes, minimum logo sizes, and font names. Several of the pantone codes and the minimum logo clearance requirement differ from the actual official guidelines.

Which TWO risks does this create for the franchise network? (Choose TWO)

options.A: Franchisees who implement the incorrect pantone codes and logo sizes will be out of compliance with actual brand standards, potentially affecting brand consistency across properties.
options.B: The memo will be rejected by franchisees because they will recognise that specific pantone codes cannot come from Claude.
options.C: Implementing incorrect brand specifications may require costly reprinting, repainting, or re-fabrication of signage and printed materials that franchisees have already produced to the wrong standard.
options.D: Claude's output will automatically overwrite the official brand guidelines stored in the company's document management system.
options.E: The brand standards manager will receive a compliance notice from Pantone for using unofficial colour codes.

items.question:
An investment operations lead at a boutique asset manager asks Claude whether a specific trading strategy falls within the exemptions available under the Investment Company Act. Claude states it does qualify, citing "Section 3(c)(7)(iii) as amended by the Investment Reform Act of 2021." When the operations lead checks with the firm's legal counsel, no such 2021 amendment exists.

What type of error did Claude make?

options.A: Claude fabricated a legislative amendment — a plausible-sounding statutory citation with an invented amendment date — that does not correspond to any real legislative event.
options.B: Claude made a staleness error — the amendment is real but was passed before 2021, so its year was incorrectly recalled.
options.C: Claude made a reasoning error — the relevant exemption exists but Claude applied the wrong analytical framework to determine eligibility.
options.D: Claude experienced a context-window limitation — the query was too complex for the model to resolve without truncating the statutory analysis.

items.question:
A quality improvement coordinator at a hospital system uses Claude to prepare a summary of the hospital's hand-hygiene compliance performance for a board quality committee presentation. Claude generates a summary that includes: "Your system achieved 94.7% hand-hygiene compliance in the most recent monitoring period, outperforming the national average of 81.3%." No compliance monitoring data was uploaded to the conversation.

Which response is MOST appropriate?

options.A: Use the national average figure (81.3%) but replace the hospital-specific figure with the real data from the monitoring system.
options.B: Verify both figures — the hospital's actual compliance rate from the monitoring system and the national benchmark from a published clinical source — before including either in the board presentation.
options.C: Use the 94.7% figure because it reflects the kind of performance that would result from the hospital's known hand-hygiene programme investments.
options.D: Ask Claude to recalculate the compliance rate using a different methodology to see if 94.7% is confirmed.

items.question:
A legal operations analyst at a precision manufacturer reviews a Claude-generated comparison of two vendor contracts uploaded as PDFs. The comparison correctly identifies price escalation clauses but also states: “Contract B contains a broad audit rights provision under Clause 18(d).” Searching Contract B, the analyst finds Clause 18(d) is a data security provision, and no audit rights clause exists at that location.

What does this finding indicate and what is the MOST appropriate immediate action?

options.A: The error indicates Claude cannot reliably compare multi-document legal agreements, and the entire comparison should be discarded and redone by a lawyer.
options.B: The error indicates a likely clause-reference substitution; the analyst should search both contracts for the actual location of any audit rights provisions rather than relying on the cited clause number.
options.C: All specific clause references in the comparison should be verified against the original contracts, since one incorrect reference indicates the response may mix real extractions with parametric clause-numbering.
options.D: The comparison should be resubmitted with a prompt asking Claude to reference page numbers so clauses can be located more easily.

items.question:
An insurance distribution manager asks Claude to summarise the coverage features of a competitor's commercial umbrella policy to prepare for a client meeting. Claude describes several coverage extensions — including a specific 'cyber event response cost' sublimit of $500,000 — that the manager cannot find in any publicly available policy form or filing for that carrier.

What should the manager conclude?

options.A: The $500,000 sublimit is likely a proprietary feature available only to large commercial accounts and not disclosed in standard policy forms.
options.B: The coverage extension was probably discontinued before the manager's inquiry and may only appear in older policy versions.
options.C: The feature and sublimit were generated from training-data patterns and may not correspond to any real coverage provision offered by that carrier.
options.D: The coverage exists but uses different terminology in the filed form; the manager should ask Claude to suggest alternative terms to search for.

items.question:
A pharmacovigilance associate at a biotech company is using Claude to help structure a literature review on adverse events associated with a class of biologics. Claude's draft review cites three specific adverse event case series — two of which can be verified in PubMed, and one of which (attributed to 'Singh et al., 2021, Journal of Clinical Safety') cannot be located anywhere.

Which THREE actions are MOST appropriate? (Choose THREE)

options.A: Remove the unverifiable case series citation from the draft immediately.
options.B: Verify the two locatable citations in full to confirm that their reported adverse event types and frequencies match what Claude attributed to them.
options.C: Assume the unverifiable citation is a database indexing lag and submit the review with a note that it is pending verification.
options.D: Conduct an independent literature search for the topic area to identify any real case series that Claude may have missed.
options.E: Accept the two verified citations as correct without further checking since they appear in PubMed.

items.question:
A brand marketing director at a specialty apparel retailer asks Claude to write a campaign brief referencing the brand's heritage and founding story. Claude produces a rich narrative that includes: "The brand was founded in 1987 by Sarah Chen, who began by hand-stitching pieces in her garage in Portland before scaling the business to its current size." The actual founding year is 1994 and the founder's name is different.

Beyond the factual errors, what is the PRIMARY concern with this type of output?

options.A: Claude generated a plausible-sounding company narrative from parametric patterns, which if used would publish false statements about real individuals and the company's history.
options.B: The founding year error (1987 vs 1994) is a minor discrepancy that can be corrected in editing without broader concern about the output's reliability.
options.C: The narrative style is too casual for a campaign brief and should be reformatted before the factual content is reviewed.
options.D: The error indicates Claude is using an outdated brand profile and should be shown the current brand history document before drafting.

items.question:
A knowledge management lead at a federal agency is advising colleagues on when to verify Claude outputs before use. She wants to give clear guidance on which content types are safest to use without extensive verification versus which always require verification.

Which pairing of content type and verification requirement is MOST accurate?

options.A: General explanations of how government procurement processes work — always requires verification against primary sources before any use.
options.B: Specific contract award dates, contractor names, and dollar values for a named procurement — always requires verification against official contract records.
options.C: Well-established principles of project management — always requires verification against PMI or PMBOK before use in training materials.
options.D: General descriptions of what a contracting officer does — requires the same verification standard as specific contract data.
